claim: Synaptic inhibition is the mechanistic backbone of maintaining network stability and modulating neuronal gain in cortical circuits.
source: Synaptic inhibition is the mechanistic backbone of a suite of cortical functions, not the least of which are maintaining network stability and modulating neuronal gain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: In cortical models with a single inhibitory neuron class, network stabilization and gain control work in opposition to one another.
source: In cortical models with a single inhibitory neuron class, network stabilization and gain control work in opposition to one another – meaning high gain coincides with low stability and vice versa.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a key finding from prior models.

claim: Cortical inhibition is diverse, with molecularly distinguished cell classes having distinct positions within the cortical circuit.
source: It is now clear that cortical inhibition is diverse, with molecularly distinguished cell classes having distinct positions within the cortical circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: In E-PV-SOM recurrently connected networks, SOM-mediated modulation can lead to simultaneous increases in neuronal gain and network stability.
source: We show how, in E – PV – SOM recurrently connected networks, SOM-mediated modulation can lead to simultaneous increases in neuronal gain and network stability.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through mathematical analysis and simulations.

claim: The impact of SOM neuron modulation depends critically on circuit connectivity and the network state.
source: Our work exposes how the impact of a modulation mediated by SOM neurons depends critically on circuit connectivity and the network state.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key conclusion of the study.

claim: The invention and widespread use of cell-specific labeling and optogenetic control occurred in the past 22 years.
source: While inhibition has been long measured (Lloyd, 1946; Hartline et al., 1956; Eccles et al., 1954), the past 22 years have witnessed a newfound appreciation of its diversity. The invention and widespread use of cell-specific labeling and optogenetic control (Fenno et al., 2011), combined with the detailed genetic and physiological characterization of cortical interneurons (Markram et al., 2004; Jiang et al., 2015) has painted a complex picture of a circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The standard cortical circuit now includes SOM and PV expressing interneuron classes at a minimum.
source: The standard cortical circuit now includes (at a minimum) SOM and PV expressing interneuron classes, with distinct synaptic interactions between these classes as well as with pyramidal neurons (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Tremblay et al., 2016; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Jiang et al., 2015; Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Inhibition has been implicated in the suppression of neuronal activity.
source: Inhibition has been implicated in the suppression of neuronal activity (Adesnik et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2017; Haider et al., 2013; Adesnik, 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Inhibition has been implicated in gain control of pyramidal neuron firing rates.
source: Inhibition has been implicated in the suppression of neuronal activity (Adesnik et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2017; Haider et al., 2013; Adesnik, 2017), gain control of pyramidal neuron firing rates (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016; Katzner et al., 2011; Ferguson and Cardin, 2020; Silver, 2010)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Inhibition must prevent runaway cortical activity that would otherwise lead to pathological activity.
source: However, inhibition must also prevent runaway cortical activity that would otherwise lead to pathological activity (Haider et al., 2013; Ozeki et al., 2009; Veit et al., 2017), enforcing constraints on how inhibition can modulate pyramidal neuron activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Increased SOM activity resulted in decreased activity in E neurons in studies of layer 2/3 mouse visual cortex.
source: Increased SOM activity resulted in decreased activity in E neurons in studies of layer 2/3 mouse visual cortex (Adesnik et al., 2012; Adesnik, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Decreased SOM activity resulted in increased E neuron activity in the piriform cortex.
source: Similarly, decreased SOM activity resulted in increased E neuron activity in the piriform cortex (Canto-Bustos et al., 2022), and other studies (Wang and Yang, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Silencing layer 4 SOM neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex resulted in decreased activity of E neurons.
source: For example, silencing layer 4 SOM neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex resulted in decreased activity of E neurons (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The key factors differentiating PV and SOM neurons in the model are that PV neurons inhibit other PV neurons while SOM neurons do not, and that PV neurons receive external (sensory) input while SOM neurons receive modulatory input.
source: The key factors differentiating PV and SOM neurons in our model are that PV neurons inhibit other PV neurons, while SOM neurons do not, and that PV neurons receive external (sensory) input while SOM neurons receive modulatory input.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the model setup.

claim: The model response is nonlinear, with neurons in each population having an expansive nonlinear transfer function.
source: The model response is nonlinear, with neurons in each population having an expansive nonlinear transfer function (Figure 1B; top, see Equation 4), consistent with many experimental reports (Priebe and Ferster, 2008; Romero-Sosa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B with supporting citations.

claim: Just two network motifs determine the sign of changes in E rates following SOM modulation.
source: Fortunately, the sum can be simplified so that just two network motifs determine the sign of changes in E rates (Figure 1C; bottom, see Equation 15).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: These motifs reflect both the disinhibitory component of the network (the SOM → PV → E and PV → PV connections) and the inhibitory component (SOM → E connections).
source: These motifs reflect both the disinhibitory component of the network (the SOM → PV → E and PV → PV connections) and the inhibitory component (SOM → E connections).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining the network motifs.

claim: Network gain is largest for high E rates and low PV rates.
source: It is immediately apparent that network gain is largest for high E rates and low PV rates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing Figure 3.

claim: Network dynamics are most stable for large PV and low E neuron rates.
source: Network dynamics are most stable for large PV and low E neuron rates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing Figure 3.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between network gain and stability, where high gain is accompanied by low stability and vice-versa.
source: In total, we have an inverse relationship between these two network features, where high gain is accompanied by low stability and vice-versa (compare heatmaps Figure 3ii and iii).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Modulation of the E-PV circuit via feedforward SOM modulation results in an inverse relationship between network gain and stability.
source: In sum, our analysis shows that modulation of the E – PV circuit via feedforward SOM modulation results in an inverse relationship between network gain and stability.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion in the Results section.

claim: Adding a recurrent connection onto SOM neurons from the E or PV neurons allows network gain and stability to change in the same direction for a SOM modulation.
source: In summary, adding a recurrent connection onto SOM neurons from the E (Figure 5) or PV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) neurons allows network gain and stability to change in the same direction for a SOM modulation.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion in the Results section with reference to figures.

claim: A negative SOM modulation can lead to increases in both network gain and stability when there is feedback from PV to SOM.
source: Similarly, in the example of a disinhibitory pathway with feedback from PV → SOM, SOM modulation can lead to changes of network gain and stability in the same direction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Here a negative SOM modulation can lead to increases in both, network gain and stability.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the disinhibitory network without feedback, a positive SOM modulation decreases stability due to increases in the mean and variance of E rates while the network gain increases.
source: For the disinhibitory network without feedback a positive SOM modulation decreases stability due to increases in the mean and variance of E rates (Figure 6Ci) while the network gain increases (Figure 6Cii).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Adding feedback PV to SOM and applying a negative SOM modulation increases both stability and gain.
source: Adding feedback PV → SOM and applying a negative SOM modulation increases both, stability and gain and, therefore, disentangles the inverse relation also in a noisy circuit (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Changing synaptic weights have often non-intuitive effects on network gain and stability.
source: In summary, changing synaptic weights have often non-intuitive effects on network gain and stability.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion in the Results section.

claim: The PV self coupling strength can have a large effect on both network gain and stability.
source: The PV self coupling strength can have a large effect on both network gain and stability (Figure 7Aiv,Biv).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 7.

claim: SOM self coupling has only minimal effect on gain and stability.
source: On the other hand, SOM self coupling has only minimal effect on gain and stability.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Tuning curve changes following from SOM modulation depend on the underlying network configuration and can differ largely in their components.
source: In sum, tuning curve changes following from SOM modulation depend on the underlying network configuration and can differ largely in their components.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion in the Results section.

claim: In a network with connections from SOM to E and SOM to PV and a feedback connection from E to SOM, modulation of SOM leads to subtractive and divisive changes at SOM and additive and multiplicative changes at E and PV populations.
source: In the example of a network with connections from SOM → E and SOM → PV and a feedback connection from E → SOM (as shown in Figure 8A), modulation of SOM leads to subtractive and divisive changes at SOM and additive and multiplicative changes at E and PV populations (Figure 8B; diamond).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 8.

claim: E neurons and PV neurons experience very similar types of inputs, both receiving excitatory drive from upstream areas.
source: First, E neurons and PV neurons experience very similar types of inputs. Both receive excitatory drive from upstream areas (Tremblay et al., 2016), and both receive strong recurrent excitation, as well as PV- and SOM-mediated inhibition (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: SOM neurons do not connect to other SOM neurons.
source: Second, SOM neurons do not connect to other SOM neurons (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Urban-Ciecko et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2015; Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The symmetry in the synaptic input to E and PV neurons allows PV neurons to dynamically track E neuron activity.
source: This symmetry in the synaptic input to E and PV neurons allows PV neurons to dynamically track E neuron activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the circuit structure.

claim: The lack of SOM neuron self-inhibition allows a high gain for any top-down modulatory signal to induce a change in E neuron response.
source: However, it is precisely the lack of SOM neuron self-inhibition that allows a high gain for any top-down modulatory signal to induce a change in E neuron response.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the circuit structure.

claim: Optogenetic perturbation of PV neurons can shift E neuron response gain.
source: However, there is also evidence for the reverse labor assignment, namely that optogenetic perturbation of PV neurons can shift E neuron response gain (Wilson et al., 2012; Atallah et al., 2012; Seybold et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: SOM neurons can suppress E neuron firing which in principle would also quench runaway E neuron activity.
source: and SOM neurons can suppress E neuron firing which in principle would also quench runaway E neuron activity (Adesnik et al., 2012; Adesnik, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The PV firing rate strongly modulates both gain and stability, often in opposing directions.
source: We show that the PV firing rate strongly modulates both gain and stability, often in opposing directions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Changing the connection strength of the E-PV subcircuit has the largest effect on network gain.
source: Similarly, changing the connection strength of the E – PV subcircuit has the largest effect on network gain (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Feedforward SOM inhibition of the E-PV circuit leads to an inverse relationship between network gain and stability.
source: A key result of our study is that feedforward SOM inhibition of the E – PV circuit leads to an inverse relationship between network gain and stability. Increases (decreases) in gain are often followed by decreases (increases) in stability (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Adding recurrent feedback onto SOM neurons can disentangle the inverse relationship between gain and stability.
source: However, adding recurrent feedback onto SOM neurons can disentangle this inverse relationship. Indeed, for many circuit parameter choices gain and stability can increase or decrease together (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Network gain depends on firing rates of E, PV, and SOM neurons at the moment of stimulus presentation.
source: An interesting observation is that network gain depends on firing rates of E, PV, and SOM neurons at the moment of stimulus presentation (Figure 3ii; Figure 4Aii, Bii, Cii; Figure 5Aii,Bii, Cii).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to multiple figures.

claim: Changes in inhibitory firing rates and changes in the behavioral state of the animal lead to gain modifications.
source: Hence any change in input to the circuit can affect the response gain to a stimulus presentation, in line with experimental evidence which suggests that changes in inhibitory firing rates and changes in the behavioral state of the animal lead to gain modifications (Ferguson and Cardin, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citation.

claim: PV neurons target both the cell bodies and proximal dendrites of both PV and E neurons.
source: PV neurons target both the cell bodies and proximal dendrites of both PV and E neurons (Markram et al., 2004; Tremblay et al., 2016; Di Cristo et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: SOM neurons inhibit the distal dendrites of E neurons.
source: In stark contrast, SOM neurons inhibit the distal dendrites of E neurons (Markram et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citation.

claim: Dendritic inhibition has been shown to gate burst responses in pyramidal neurons greatly reducing cellular gain.
source: Dendritic inhibition has been shown to gate burst responses in pyramdial neurons greatly reducing cellular gain (Larkum et al., 2004; Mehaffey et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Dendritic inhibition is localized near the synaptic site for E to E coupling.
source: Furthermore, dendritic inhibition is localized near the synaptic site for E → E coupling, and modeling (Yang et al., 2016) and experimental (Adler et al., 2019) work shows how such dendritic inhibition can control E synapse plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: SOM neurons may be an important modulator not only of cortical response but also of learning.
source: This implies that SOM neurons may be an important modulator not only of cortical response but also of learning.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from cited work.

claim: The E-PV-SOM cortical circuit is best characterized in superficial layers of sensory neocortex.
source: The E – PV – SOM cortical circuit is best characterized in superficial layers of sensory neocortex (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Tremblay et al., 2016; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Cell densities and connectivity patterns of interneuron populations change across the brain and across cortical layers.
source: However, cell densities and connectivity patterns of interneuron populations change across the brain (Kim et al., 2017) and across cortical layers (Tremblay et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Small changes in synaptic strength can switch the sign of how SOM modulation affects rates.
source: However, the exact synaptic strength of a connection relative to the strength of all other connection strengths in the circuit is an important determinant of circuit response. Small changes can switch the sign of how SOM modulation affects rates (Figure 1C and D) or change the stability and network gain of the circuit (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to figures.

claim: Short-term synaptic dynamics in cortical circuits often show net depression.
source: Short-term synaptic dynamics in cortical circuits often show net depression (Zucker and Regehr, 2002)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citation.

claim: The E to SOM connection facilitates with increasing pre-synaptic activity.
source: however, the E → SOM connection facilitates with increasing pre-synaptic activity (Tremblay et al., 2016; Reyes et al., 1998; Thomson, 1997; Yavorska and Wehr, 2016; Beierlein et al., 2003; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Prolonged activation of E neurons recruits SOM activity through facilitation of the E to SOM synapse.
source: Indeed, prolonged activation of E neurons recruits SOM activity through this facilitation (Beierlein et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citation.

claim: Optogenetically decreasing SOM activity leads to mostly additive and multiplicative tuning curve changes in the mouse primary auditory cortex.
source: Specifically, optogenetically decreasing SOM activity leads to mostly additive and multiplicative tuning curve changes in the mouse primary auditory cortex (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016), which in our model follows from strong E to SOM feedback.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citation.

claim: The study is based on a linearization approach, which only allows investigation of circuit dynamics close to a stable network state.
source: Our study is based on a linearization approach, which only allows us to investigate the circuit dynamics close to a stable network state.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: The results hold in the case with noisy inputs.
source: While this makes our results mathematically tractable and more intuitive and we confirm that our results hold in the case with noisy inputs (Figure 6)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 6.

claim: VIP neurons strongly connect to SOM cells, forming a disinhibitory pathway.
source: VIP neurons strongly connect to SOM cells, forming a disinhibitory pathway (Pi et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The nonlinear transfer functions are described by a power law.
source: The nonlinear transfer functions are described by a power law.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: The system is stable if the real parts of all three eigenvalues of the Jacobian are negative.
source: The system is stable if the real parts of all three Eigenvalues of the Jacobian are negative.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.

claim: The stability measure ignores the oscillatory behavior of the system (i.e. the imaginary part of the eigenvalues).
source: This stability measure ignores the oscillatory behavior of the system (i.e. the imaginary part of the eigenvalues).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section.
